title: Seek the city's peace (Jeremiah 29:4–11)
hook: to exiles: build houses, plant gardens, pray for the city you're in

segments.voice: Yesterday, the spoiled vessel remade on the wheel, and your line was the potter starts again. What did you put back on the wheel? Day four hundred seventy-five.

A letter arrives in Babylon. It has come hundreds of miles from Jerusalem, carried by royal messengers. The people reading it are exiles: priests, craftsmen, families, taken from home along with King Jeconiah, living now in the capital of the empire that conquered them. And they're restless. Some prophets are telling them not to unpack; in Jerusalem, one has promised it will all be over within two years. The letter is from Jeremiah, back in Jerusalem. Everyone leans in. Surely he'll tell them how to hold on, how to resist, how soon they'll be free. Today, what the letter actually said.
screen: `A LETTER TO BABYLON.` → `EXILES, RESTLESS.` → `DON'T UNPACK, SAY SOME.` → `WHAT DID JEREMIAH WRITE?`

segments.voice: Unpack, says Jeremiah. In the King James Bible: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them." Marry. Have children. Let your children marry. Grow there, don't shrink. And then the line that must have stunned them: "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." Pray for Babylon. The city whose army marched you away from home. The word for peace here is shalom, and it means much more than no war. Shalom is wholeness, welfare, everything being as it should: enough food, safe streets, healthy families, right relationships. Seek Babylon's shalom, because your shalom is tied up in it. Jeremiah also warns them not to listen to the prophets promising a quick return. It will be seventy years, he says, a lifetime. Then comes a verse you may have seen on graduation cards and coffee mugs: "For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end." Thoughts of shalom. It's a beautiful promise, and it's worth knowing its first setting: written to a whole community, to be kept through seventy years of exile, most of whom would not live to see the return. It's a promise for the long haul, not the next week. Jewish communities in the centuries since have often prayed for the welfare of the countries they lived in, and many Christians have read this letter as a guide for living faithfully in any place that isn't quite home.
screen: `BUILD HOUSES, PLANT GARDENS.` · `PRAY FOR BABYLON.` · `SHALOM: WHOLENESS, WELFARE.` · `SEVENTY YEARS: A LONG PROMISE.` · then, large: `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your town, or hold it in mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture the place where you live now, whether it feels like home or not. Its streets, its schools, its hospital, its traffic, its people who annoy you. Picture its mayor or council, whether or not you voted for them. Then picture one place in it that isn't whole: a closed shop, a shelter, a struggling school, a lonely street. Hold that place gently. Wish it shalom. If you pray, you can pray for your city by name. The bell holds the time.
Shalom. Peace as wholeness and welfare: what Jeremiah told exiles to seek and pray for, even in the city that took them captive.
Your line: pray for your city. Today, do one small thing for the shalom of where you live: pick up litter, shop local, thank a city worker, or learn a neighbor's name. Day four hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Many churches pray each Sunday for their city, nation and leaders, and Jeremiah 29:7 is often cited as the reason; in many synagogues a prayer for the welfare of the government is said on the Sabbath.

original.note: Hebrew: peace, wholeness, welfare. still a greeting in Hebrew today.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jeremiah 29:11 is a personal promise about my career plans.
what it means: a letter telling exiles to settle in, seek their captors' city's shalom, and trust God through a seventy-year wait.
what a scholar hears: the word shalom appears three times in verse seven. the letter answers rival prophets, like Hananiah, who promised a return within two years.

notes: Audit (y2 second sample): 'the city that burned your Temple' was an anachronism: the letter (29:1–3, under Zedekiah, after Jeconiah's exile in 597 BC) came years before Babylon burned the Temple in 587/586 BC; rewritten. 'First wave of deportations' replaced with the text's own marker (29:2, Jeconiah); 'across the desert' softened, since the route ran along the Fertile Crescent; the practice's 'whoever you voted for' clarified.
The letter went with Elasah and Gemariah, envoys of King Zedekiah (29:3); 'royal messengers' in the voice. Confirm.
'Two years' is Hananiah's prophecy in 28:3 (in Jerusalem); 29:8–9 warns against prophets among the exiles. The hook places the two-year promise in Jerusalem, as in 28:3. Confirm.
Shalom appears three times in 29:7 (KJV 'peace' twice; Hebrew shalom three times, counting 'in the peace thereof shall ye have peace'). Confirm the count.
Jewish prayer for the government (e.g. Hanoten Teshuah) traced in part to Jeremiah 29:7 and Pirkei Avot 3:2. Confirm.
